weakness: The pipeline assumed the charger rests on its bottom face: the top grasp took the base's y axis projected on the horizontal as the closing direction, which is degenerate when the charger lies on its side, and the only in-hand pose it can insert from is the upright one. A side-lying charger needs a regrasp (roll 90 deg and put it down), and that regrasp was not made reliable within 6 repair iterations.
how_found: Questioned A1 (orientation): the grasp code zeroes the z component of a body axis and normalizes it, which only makes sense if that axis is horizontal. Tipped-over parts are common on real tables.
why_missed: Phase 1 only saw the task's own randomization (yaw only), so every grasp computation silently relied on the object being upright, and the insertion was built around one in-hand pose.
fix: Not recovered (best 0.3 on v1, debug evals). Tried: (1) oriented-box top grasp: grasp works but the rolled in-hand pose puts the 20 cm hand vertically at receptacle height and it hits the table; (2-4) roll in the air and release: the hand cannot get low with the closing axis vertical, the part rides on the lower finger or drops 10 cm and lands upside down; (5) grasp across the part's long axis with a 45 deg approach that bisects world-down before and after the roll, then place it 2 mm above the table: lands upright in one roll on most seeds; (6) check each move's endpoint and re-plan, pitch the insertion grasp away from the receptacle. Remaining failures: the regrasp sometimes closes on nothing although move_to reported success, the part is flung when the hand re-plans while holding it, and the extra moves exhaust the 2000-step budget. Pipeline reverted to the Phase 1 version; last attempt kept in wip/pipeline_v1_repair6.py.
general_rule: When the required in-hand pose cannot be grasped directly from the object's resting pose, plan the regrasp as a place, not a drop: choose a grasp axis that stays horizontal through the reorientation and an approach that is clear of the support surface both before and after it, and verify after every grasp that the object is actually held before continuing.

weakness: The grasp was computed once from the detections taken at t=0 and executed open loop. The charger was pushed ~26 mm just as the hand arrived, so the fingers closed on the moving part: it slid in the grip and was held at its peg end, and the fingers then struck the receptacle face 16 mm before full insertion (0.4).
how_found: Questioned A3: the only perception before contact happened at the start of the episode, and nothing re-checks the object before the gripper closes. Objects on a real table get bumped or settle.
why_missed: In the base task nothing moves, so one (very well averaged) measurement was always valid; accuracy was optimised, freshness was never considered. The pipeline also treated 'gripper is holding something' as success of the grasp, though the insertion depends on where in the hand the part sits.
fix: At the pre-grasp pose, wait until two averaged estimates 0.25 s apart agree (object at rest), compare with the pose the grasp was planned from, and re-plan the grasp if it moved more than 3 mm. After closing: require gripper_holding, and after lifting compare the measured in-hand pose with the planned one; if it is more than 8 mm off, put the part down and regrasp. Recovered 1.0 on base and v2.
general_rule: Re-observe the target immediately before committing to contact and only act on a measurement taken while it is at rest; after grasping, check that the object sits in the hand where the plan assumed, not merely that something is held.

weakness: Every free-space move was a straight screw motion planned for the bare arm against an empty world: after lifting the charger 5 cm the pipeline moved straight to the pre-insertion pose, dragging the charger and fingers through a 9 cm wall between the pick and place areas (0.0; the official oracle also scored 0.0).
how_found: Questioned A7: no move_to call passed avoid=, and the lift height (5 cm) was chosen for the empty task table, not for what stands between start and goal. Real workspaces have trays, rims and other objects between pick and place locations.
why_missed: The base scene has nothing but the two task objects, so the shortest path was always free; and the planner's own collision model covers the arm only, so even an obstacle-aware call would not have protected the part hanging below the fingers.
fix: transfer(): treat every non-task object as an obstacle (averaged oriented boxes from get_obstacles), rise vertically to 5 cm above the highest obstacle top, travel at that height, then descend onto the pre-insertion pose, all with avoid=; the pre-grasp move also avoids non-task objects. Also found while repairing: gripper_holding() read False right after closing on a good grasp (contact registers a few steps later), so the v2 miss-handling lifted and later dropped a held part; now it waits up to 0.5 s for the signal and opens the gripper before retreating after a real miss. Recovered 1.0 on base, v2, v3.
general_rule: Plan free-space moves for the arm plus whatever it is holding: clear obstacles by the held object's extent below the gripper (e.g. rise above the tallest obstacle, travel, then descend) instead of trusting a straight-line or arm-only collision check.

weakness: With a 0.3 kg, low-friction charger in hand the arm settled a few mm below and ~0.01 rad off its commanded pose. The servo loop removed this offset while holding still in front of the receptacle, but every new servo call started again from the uncompensated command, so the 6 mm insertion stroke brought the pegs ~3 mm low onto the receptacle face (0.0; oracle 0.0). The part did not actually slip in the fingers.
how_found: Questioned A9/A10 (in-hand slip, a light grippy part); diagnosis with the true in-hand pose showed the hold constant and the error coming from the arm's load-dependent tracking offset instead.
why_missed: With the light default part the arm's steady-state error was well under the 0.5 mm clearance, so per-move feedback that restarted from the nominal command looked sufficient; the integral correction was local to one call and its learned value was thrown away.
fix: servo_to re-measures the in-hand pose after every free-space move and, when the part's orientation is off by more than 0.005 rad, shifts the full commanded pose by (last command vs pose reached); the free-space position offset (command minus reached) is stored and added to every later command, including the contact-phase insertion steps. Two earlier attempts (re-aiming to the same nominal pose; integral re-aim without carrying the offset) did not converge. Recovered 1.0 on base, v2, v3, v4.
general_rule: Treat the controller's steady-state tracking error under the current load as a calibration: measure command-versus-reached in free space just before a precision move and carry that offset into the contact moves, instead of re-commanding nominal targets after each correction.

weakness: The pipeline assumed the part's yaw is within +-60 deg of the insertion direction. With the charger reversed (pegs toward the robot) the hand must turn it ~180 deg about the vertical between grasp and insertion, which no grasp choice avoids: on some seeds the wrist hit its joint range and the planner stopped short while reporting success, on others the insertion jammed (0.0; oracle 0.0).
how_found: Questioned A12: the grasp was chosen to minimise wrist rotation at pick time, never checking the rotation needed later at the goal. A part put down the wrong way round is common.
why_missed: The task's yaw range kept the pick-to-place rotation small, so the grasp heuristic (closing aligned with the current TCP y) was always also fine for the insertion.
fix: If the yaw error to the insertion direction exceeds 60 deg, turn the charger on the table first: pick it up 3 cm, turn it by at most 90 deg about the vertical, put it down, re-detect, repeat. Grasp candidates (both closing directions, and for turning-only grasps both lean directions) are tried until move_checked confirms the pre-grasp pose was really reached. The insertion grasp's 15 deg pitch now always leans toward the pegs so the palm stays clear of the receptacle (same finding as in v1). Recovered 1.0 on base, v2-v5 (5 repair iterations).
general_rule: Before committing to a grasp, check that the whole sequence it implies (pick, carry, final pose) stays within the arm's joint range; if the required reorientation is too large, reorient the object in steps through place-and-regrasp, and verify that each motion actually reached its target instead of trusting the planner's success flag.
